Paul Graham didn't say that. It was Patrick Collison's remark, and the interviewer (YC Visiting Partner Vivian Shen) brought it up with PG. She also supplied the reasons: money is easy to raise, and you can "spin out a bunch of agents." PG disagreed with it.

**Verdict:** PG says lean startups aren't dead. You can still start a startup on not much money, because technology, AI tokens included, always gets cheaper.

**Based on:** something he said (Sept 2026 interview, [yt-5bxp78i96S8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8))

**Why he says it**
- **He doesn't use the term "lean startup."** "I've never really been clear what what a lean startup is." He hasn't read *The Lean Startup* and says YC was already funding that kind of startup before the book. He asked Shen to define it, and she said "starting with just a little bit of money on a very focused area." He answered that version. ([@ 10:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=630s))
- **Starting cheap still works.** "I think there's a lot of things you can do for cheap." Tokens are "very expensive at the moment, but that's just cuz there's a shortage of GPUs." He expects inference prices at a given quality to fall "like 30x a year or something like that." ([@ 11:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=664s))
- **"everything technology always gets cheaper… I think you can still start a startup on not much money."** ([@ 11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=697s))
- **This includes rockets.** "you adjust for how much money you've got." You can't build the rocket yet, but you can design it, simulate it and show it to experts, then raise money for the next stage. "As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more." ([@ 12:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s))
- **He doesn't think AI has changed much about startups.** "so far almost everything is exactly the same." The only new thing is "giant AI bills… tens of thousands of dollars a day in tokens." That's the cost he expects to fall. ([@ 16:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=998s))

**What he didn't address:** Nothing in the vault has him talking about running agents in parallel. He didn't respond to that part of the question at all.

**What would change his answer:** He would only expect starting cheap to get harder if technology stopped getting cheaper. He also notes that a famous expert can raise on a white paper, because they come "with automatic cred." A new graduate can't do that, so they need to reach a real milestone first.

Other YC people in the vault see a bigger shift from AI. Seibel and Caldwell are revising their MVP advice, and Tan claims 400x leverage from agents. That's another view, and it isn't what PG said.

Garry Tan didn't say it. In the vault, Sam Altman says it to Tan, at Startup School 2026 (YC channel, 2026-07-28), and he notes that Tan probably *couldn't* say it himself.

**Verdict:** Altman's reason is network effects. YC brings together the people you'll later start companies with, so as it gets bigger its lead over everyone else keeps growing.

**Based on:** said it (by Altman, not Tan)

**Why he says it**
- He says it while answering how to find co-founders. Five to ten years earlier, he says, the main limit on how many good startups YC could fund was co-founder matching: "five or 10 years ago, what felt like was limiting the number of good startups YC could fund is figuring out how to solve the co-founder matching problem." ([yt-ZIaOBAjvc38 @ 16:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=985s))
- He says the old fix was moving to the Bay Area, but he's less sure about that now: "I still think that's probably good advice, although I feel like I have less of an intuition for it now." (@ [16:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s))
- Then comes the claim. In the raw transcript (auto-captions) it runs: "I can say this, Gary probably can't. I I I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before. Uh, the distance between like YC and second place is has expanded. And this is a reminder of the power of network effects." (@ 16:56 to 17:28)
- His point is that the network compounds over many years. He met his OpenAI co-founders "like many many years in some cases before uh starting OpenAI", so "the sooner you can put yourself just in a flow where you're going to meet the people that will be your eventual co-founders … I I think the better." (@ [17:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1048s))

**What Tan does say:** In the same talk he says the network is a big part of why YC works, but he doesn't compare YC with anyone else: "this is the kind of like loose network and the spirit of helping each other and this like very long-term outlook has been an awesome thing." (@ 23:35)

**Supporting view from Paul Graham:** In a September 2026 essay, PG says YC has network effects it never planned: "YC itself is an instance of network effects in something you wouldn't expect to have them. We didn't intend it to be, but we realized very quickly that that was what we'd stumbled upon." ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]])

**Caveat:** This is YC's former president speaking at YC's own event. "Gary probably can't" admits the conflict of interest: Tan runs YC, so he can't credibly make this claim about it. In the vault the claim is backed by the network-effects argument, not by data comparing YC with other accelerators.

**Verdict:** No. Nothing in the YC vault shows Dalton Caldwell recommending Portugal's Startup Visa or Lisbon. He doesn't mention Portugal, Lisbon or any visa program anywhere in it, so the premise has nothing behind it.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault. I searched for Portugal, Lisbon, visa and immigration in both the wiki and the raw transcripts, and checked the timeline for "visa". All came back with nothing from Caldwell, or from any other member.

**What the vault does say about where to base a startup**, from other YC people, not Caldwell:
- Paul Graham (April 2026, speaking in Stockholm) says founders should go to the field's center, which for startups is Silicon Valley, at least for a while: "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 0:36, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s)
- Sam Altman (July 2026) agrees, less firmly. He says moving to the Bay Area has been the best way to find co-founders, but he has less of an intuition for it now ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]]).
- Caldwell's material in the vault covers ideas, co-founders, fundraising, MVPs and ambition. None of it is about location or immigration.

**My best guess, not from the vault:** If Caldwell were asked "Lisbon via Portugal's Startup Visa, or the Bay Area?", the YC default would point to the Bay Area. That comes from PG's and Altman's statements, not from anything Caldwell said, so don't attribute it to him.

**Gap:** `sources.yaml` lists PG's essay "The Founder Visa" (paulgraham.com/foundervisa.html), but it hasn't been compiled into the wiki. It's about a proposed US founder visa, not Portugal, so it wouldn't change this answer either way.

I found nothing in the YC vault on either question, so there's no verdict from Tan I can give you.

**Based on:** beyond the vault, plus my own guess

**What I checked:** I searched the compiled wiki and the raw transcripts for "crowdfunding", "Regulation Crowdfunding", "Reg CF", "SEC", "SAFE", "accredited investor", "convertible" and "valuation cap", and checked SAFE in the timeline. There were no relevant statements. The only hits were general remarks about regulated industries (Seibel on MVPs) and the everyday word "safe". The vault has two Tan talks from 2026: the Altman conversation at Startup School and *Own Your Intelligence*. Neither touches securities law or how to structure a fundraise.

**On the Reg CF cap:** The vault has nothing on this, and I don't have a statement from Tan on raising the cap that I'm sure of, so I won't make one up. If you have a specific post or interview in mind, add it as a source and compile it, and I can answer from it with citations.

**On Reg CF instead of SAFEs:**
- **The question mixes two things (not in the vault).** Reg CF is an SEC exemption that lets you raise from the public through a registered portal. A SAFE is a type of security. You can issue SAFEs under Reg CF (portals sell "Crowd SAFEs"), so the real choice is who you raise from, not which document you sign.
- **Where the SAFE comes from (not in the vault).** YC created the SAFE in 2013 and uses it as its standard seed document. YC's leadership is very unlikely to tell founders to drop it.
- **My guess, labelled as one:** For a seed-stage company aiming for venture scale, YC people would most likely tell you to raise on SAFEs from a few fast, experienced investors. A crowd round of hundreds of small investors is slower, costs more and adds disclosure obligations. The closest documented principles are general:
  - PG (2014): the way to convince investors is to be doing well and say so ([[fundraising/investors/how-to-convince-investors]]).
  - PG (April 2026): Valley investors decide fast because they compete for deals ([[fundraising/investors/why-valley-investors-decide-faster]]).
  - Caldwell and Seibel (2026): don't spend months on fundraising ([[startups/strategy/building-leverage-before-negotiating]]).

  None of these mentions crowdfunding, and none is from Tan. My guess would flip for a consumer company with a large, loyal user base that wants customers as owners, but no vault member has said so.

If Tan's views on this matter to you, I can look for his posts or interviews on Reg CF and accredited-investor rules and add them to the vault as sources.

**The premise is wrong. In the vault, Livingston says nearly the opposite.** She did use "aggressive" and "ruthless", but she was describing the *investors* of that era, not the founders YC backed. She presents herself as the contrast to them:

> "it felt like a family and I was its mom I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless - for a couple of them that I know I cared about how founders were feeling if they were overwhelmed if they were eating properly" ([yt-8d-cApFHjeY @ 17:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s); 2018 talk, *9 Things She Learned From Founding YC*)

**Based on:** said it. She speaks to this directly.

**What she actually screened for (her part of the interview was judging character):**
- Earnestness, determination, flexibility, and above all the co-founder relationship: "did they seem earnest did they seem determined were they flexible minded and most importantly what was the relationship between the co-founders like" ([@ 14:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s))
- "from the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" (@ 14:51)
- She turned people away for arrogance: "if I could tell someone was a conceited we did not fund them … early on I was pretty rigid about this and I think that's the basis of the culture of our alumni community" ([@ 15:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=927s))
- In 2024 she added that the founders she has known were smart, curious, determined and above all independent-minded: "you cannot be conventional minded to start a startup with a brand new idea" (yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 51:09)

**Why she thought this worked:** at YC's stage there were no growth figures or market sizes to go on, so "we had to judge the founders not by what they were but what they could turn into" (@ 16:35). The partners judged the idea. She judged whether the people were earnest and whether the founding team would hold together. She also believed that early strictness shaped the culture of the whole alumni network.

**Probably where the idea came from:** the closest thing in the vault is Paul Graham's word "formidable", which he says comes from his and Jessica's private vocabulary. He defines it as someone who "gets what they want, in any situation". Investors like that, he says, because "If they get what they want, you get what you want" (yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 9:57). That's about being effective, not ruthless, and the explanation is PG's, not Livingston's.

One caveat: the vault has two Livingston sources (2018 and 2024). Neither has her endorsing ruthless founders, but I can't rule out that she said something like it elsewhere. If you have a source for that quote, I can add it to the vault and check it.
